Indexing makes one language-model call per passage, retrieval makes none, and deleting a document is a database operation with no model calls. On the full 11,402-passage MuSiQue corpus we verify that, after deleting 10% of the documents, the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. We compare Lightfoot with HippoRAG 2, LightRAG and fast-graphrag under identical extraction, answer and embedding models on MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA. Lightfoot builds the cheapest index on all three datasets, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2 and 3-6x below LightRAG and fast-graphrag. Against HippoRAG 2 it is significantly better on MuSiQue retrieval (+2.8 points recall@5 and +4.3 recall@10 on a held-out split) and on HotpotQA answers (+7.7 points exact match), and significantly worse on 2WikiMultiHopQA (-3.9 recall@2, -8.4 F1). Deleting the same documents took LightRAG 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours; fast-graphrag has no deletion path. Code and per-question results: https://github.com/udayallu-ml/Lightfoot-GraphRAG

title: GradReason: LLMs as Meta-Learners that Replace Training Epochs with Training-Data-Free Weight Updates
abstract: Standard training recipes make a fixed number of passes over the training data, even when an epoch mostly adds mini-batch noise. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that reads the weight and gradient history of a run can replace some of these epochs with updates that compute no gradient and read no training image. In GradReason, an LLM agent is called every ten epochs. In a restricted sandbox, it analyses recent weight snapshots, epoch-mean gradients, and validation metrics, then submits a Python program that computes new weights and a plan marking each of the next ten epochs as data or virtual. A virtual epoch is kept only if it passes a forward-only check on 5,000 held-out validation images. In 120 runs on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with three architectures, Claude Opus 5.5 used 32.8% fewer data epochs than the 80-epoch recipe at 0.31 percentage points lower test accuracy (95% CI -0.72 to +0.09; 0.94 points on ResNet-18), on the recipe's own frontier of data against accuracy. Unprompted, Opus averaged recent weight snapshots in every run. This choice produced the savings: a fixed rule with the same acceptance check but extrapolations from prior work saved 5.4% of the data epochs, and the same rule with averaging added saved 25.0%. The LLM's contribution is to find a working update within a single run; once found, a fixed rule implements it equally well. An Opus run cost 0.68 USD, but at this scale the agent's latency exceeded the GPU time it saved.

title: The forces at hand: social learning is permissive, not instructive, for the evolution of phenotypic plasticity
abstract: Evolution can favour a trait for two reasons: an instructive cause makes selection favour the trait; a permissive one lets it persist once selection no longer removes it. The distinction matters most for phenotypic plasticity and its replacement by inherited behaviour, genetic assimilation, the Baldwin effect. Social learning is credited with favouring plasticity on evidence that cannot tell the two apart: how much plasticity remains at the end of a simulation. Here we show, analytically and computationally, which role it plays in a minimal model of learning and evolution. Writing expected fitness as a function of plasticity, we find that environmental change is the only source of benefit from plasticity, and the social channel enters only its cost. Simulation confirms this: in a static environment selection against plasticity never reverses sign at any channel strength; when the environment changes, it reverses at a threshold the channel lowers, and without the channel the population collapses before reaching it. Social learning is permissive, not instructive: it supplies the means to be plastic, never the reason. For the debate over whether plasticity leads evolution, this is one case settled by measurement: environmental change directs, socially inherited information permits, and neither suffices alone.
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures. Code and archived outputs: https://github.com/drnamlabs-gif/forces-at-hand

title: Network Contention State Aware Dynamic Optimizer for Accelerator Collective Communication Libraries
abstract: Collective Communication Libraries (CCL) are critical for large-scale distributed AI/ML training, yet their configurations are determined by static heuristics that do not account for real-time network conditions. Our empirical study shows that these heuristics perform near-optimally in contention-free environments, but degrade substantially under background traffic. To address this, we present a cooperative multi-agent run-time optimizer for accelerator collective communication. Our approach employs a two-agent architecture: (i) detector- a Long Short Term Memory(LSTM) recurring neural network fed classifier head with a sequential probability ratio test that distinguishes sustained contention from transient spikes; and (ii) selector- a configuration selector built on a Dueling Double DQN (D3QN) with Conservative Q-Learning that adapts configuration parameters in response. We implemented this dynamic tuner over NCCL, a widely used CCL developed by NVIDIA. When evaluated on Chameleon Cloud's isolated bare-metal cluster, this dynamic tuning approach reduces AllReduce latency by 36% over NCCL and 32% over a fully converged AutoCCL. We further evaluated it across six real AI workloads spanning convolutional networks, transformers, and recommendation architectures. Our multi-agent tuner approach delivers up to 65% speedups on Delta cluster with NVIDIA A100 GPUs and Slingshot-11 fabric internode connectivity.

title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
abstract: Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges $c$ per token processed and $β$ per pair attended. Their ratio $P^*=c/β$ is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.

title: SWEET: Mitigating Spurious Feature Reliance in LLM Reasoning via Weight Editing
abstract: Reasoning in large language models can be disrupted by simple input perturbations (e.g. adding irrelevant distractors), suggesting reliance on spurious correlations. Identifying and suppressing the spurious features involved in long chain-of-thought reasoning remains challenging. We introduce Spurious-feature WEight EdiTing (SWEET), a training-free method that combines counterfactual interventions with mechanistic interpretability to identify and suppress spurious-features. SWEET extracts token- and sequence-level behavioral directions from activation contrasts between original problems and their counterfactual variants - capturing local and global patterns of spurious reasoning. It then localizes the responsible MLP neurons and attention heads and suppresses their contributions along these directions through weight edits. Using only 20 original-counterfactual pairs for direction extraction, SWEET improves accuracy by an average of 11.8 percentage points on perturbed inputs and 2 points on original inputs across five open-weight reasoning models and five reasoning benchmarks. It also reduces the relative gap between original and perturbed accuracies from 17.6% to 2.5%. Analyses identify two recurring forms of spurious reasoning, i.e. over-integrating irrelevant conditions and overthinking, and provide mechanistic evidence that SWEET improves reasoning robustness by suppressing both behavioral directions.

title: Improving Analytic Constants via Interpretable AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
abstract: AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as partially-formalized Lean blueprints: human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas, and theorems. An AI agent then iteratively refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure, allowing local improvements to automatically propagate to a verified final bound. This interpretable structure allows humans to inspect the agent's refinements and understand how local improvements propagate to the final theorem. For Grothendieck's constant ($\mathcal{K}_G$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_G \leq \fracπ{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})} - 10^{-17}, $$ an explicit numerical improvement over Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant ($\mathcal{K}_K$), we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_K \geq 0.356565, $$ improving Wang's 2025 bound of $0.3554$. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of both partial formalization and iterative agentic refinement for interpretable mathematical discovery.

title: Hybrid Source Code Change Impact Analysis
abstract: Change impact analysis (CIA) helps developers identify code entities impacted by their initial changes. While several approaches for CIA were proposed, they still struggle with either low precision or low recall, thereby increasing manual effort for developers to verify the results. Furthermore, limitations in the used datasets and experimental setups can bias the results reported by many CIA approaches. In this paper, we first address the dataset limitations by manually labeling 1,931 changed code entities stemming from 263 commits of 22 open-source Java projects. Next, we introduce two variants of katIA, our code change impact analysis approach that combines static impact analysis with the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The first variant uses a single prompt (katIA-SP) for refining an initial static impact set while the second variant uses three specialized agents (katIA-MA). The evaluation with our curated dataset shows that katIA-SP with Gemini 2.5 Flash achieved an F1-score of 22.4% when matching impacted entities by their fully qualified names (FQN) and 27.0% when matching them by their class and entity names (CE). The latter shows an improvement of 2.0 percentage points over the state-of-the-art. This score is further improved by katIA-MA which, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, yields an FQN-matching F1-score of 29.1% and a CE-matching F1-score of 33.3%. While these improvements come at the cost of increased median generation time from 0.570 s to 11.214 s and median token usage from 1,235 to 6,462 tokens, the improved performance justifies the additional cost. The comparison of three LLMs using katIA-SP finds that Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most consistent model. These results indicate that combining static impact analysis with LLM-based refinement, particularly with the multi-agent variant, can improve code change impact analysis.

title: Validating AI-Discovered Cloud Threats on Live Infrastructure: A Multi-Model, Multi-Cloud Study
abstract: Cloud infrastructure threat modeling lacks empirical validation of AI-discovered threats. We present a three-phase methodology of multi-agent threat discovery, automated exploit synthesis, and non-destructive live validation, and apply it to three commercial foundation models on two cloud architectures, validating each threat natively on the cloud (AWS, GCP, or Azure) it was discovered against. Of 233 AI-discovered threats, 103 were confirmed and 34 refuted (75.2\% precision, 95\% CI [67.3, 81.7]); 44 were conditional (the named mechanism refuted but an equivalent impact shown through another path) and 52 indeterminate. Multi-model discovery helped through breadth, not agreement: the three models together found 2.2$\times$ the confirmed threats of the best single model at comparable precision, while threats reported by several models were confirmed no more often than single-model ones. False positives were not architecture-specific: they asserted access or system state the deployment did not have. Threats coded in advance as observable configuration resolved cleanly more often than multi-step behavioral threats (72.5\% vs.\ 51.6\%), which were more often conditional, suggesting that models more often misidentify the exploitation mechanism than the underlying weakness. AI-assisted discovery is a practical input to security workflows when paired with empirical validation.

title: DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
abstract: Existing evaluations of AI models on high-finance work focus on retrieving answers from financial documents and producing numerically correct outputs. Real private equity (PE) and investment banking (IB) work also depends on choosing between conflicting sources, making sound assumptions, and keeping every step auditable. We introduce DeepFinance, an ultra long-horizon benchmark of 21 end-to-end PE and IB tasks that take a human professional an average of 27.1 hours. Each task pairs a request with a data room averaging 19 files and is graded against an average of 84 expert-written rubric criteria covering output, workflow, and judgment. We evaluate 22 model configurations, each in its native agent harness. The best configuration, GPT-6 Astra with max reasoning, satisfies 57.6% of rubric criteria, and the top four configurations are not statistically distinguishable. Frontier models often calculate correctly from the wrong inputs and find decision-relevant evidence without acting on it.

title: Remembering to Reason: Structured Memory for Scene and Workflow Understanding in Robot-Assisted Surgery
abstract: Surgical video understanding is an important foundation for intelligent assistance in robot-assisted surgery. Similar surgical views can reflect different actions or procedural stages. Interpreting these views requires access to earlier observations, yet frame-centric prompting leaves this history unavailable. We introduce MemSurg, a framework that remembers surgical observations before reasoning over them. Its structured memory graph stores timestamped entity categories, locations, motion cues, and interaction summaries. Chronological links preserve recent context, while entity-associated links connect recurring observations across the procedure. Task-adaptive retrieval then supplies evidence-grounded prompts for scene and workflow reasoning, supporting both frozen inference and memory-conditioned supervised fine-tuning. Evaluation on robot-assisted prostatectomy and two complementary surgical benchmarks shows a 10.43-percentage-point gain over SurgRAW with GPT-4o. Memory conditioning adds 6.52 points under matched Qwen3-VL-8B fine-tuning, and an inference-time plug-in adds 7.04 points to EndoChat. These results support structured memory as a reusable source of procedural evidence for surgical video understanding. Our code will be publicly released.

title: Towards A Parametrized Complexity of Determinization
abstract: Given a nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA), we want to estimate the difficulty of finding an equivalent deterministic finite automaton (DFA). We demonstrate that computing the state complexity of an NFA within polynomial precision is \textsf{PSPACE}-hard, and furthermore the same holds for the complexity of the subset construction, Brzozowski's algorithm, or, indeed, \emph{any} determinization algorithm which runs at least as fast. This result implies that making any \textit{a priori} estimate of the running time of the major determinization algorithms is inherently hard. To circumvent this---in the spirit of parametrized complexity---we try to identify complexity measures which can guarantee efficient determinization. Our main idea rests on linking the complexity of the subset construction to transition monoids using the semigroup complexity. We show that the semigroup complexity by itself can be reasonably approximated for certain classes of NFAs, and then introduce \emph{subset complexity}---a refinement of the semigroup complexity which has a tighter connection with the subset construction. In certain scenarios, the subset complexity can be approximated in polynomial time, making it potentially viable for more practical applications.

title: Beyond Real or Fake: A Dual-Channel Authenticity and Reasoning Protocol for Photographic Assessment
abstract: Forensic verification has converged on a binary "real vs. fake" label that confates fully synthetic, tampered, and AI-retouched images despite their very different consequences. We argue that GenAI manipulations decompose along two complementary channels: a camera channel of sensor fingerprints (destroyed by neural processing), and a semantic channel of scene-level coherence (disrupted by content edits). Each manipulation type leaves a distinctive two-channel signature. We instantiate this taxonomy in 2CAP (2-Channel Authenticity Protocol), pairing a contrastively-trained camera encoder with a frozen semantic encoder to serve two applications on a shared backbone: (i) four-class authenticity classification via cross-attention fusion with learnable reliability weights; and (ii) evidence generation, where an authentic image serves as a reference for a query and the two encoders produce per-channel alignment scores together with a patch-level saliency map. These signals are supplied as privileged context to a frozen Vision-Language Model (VLM) through an Observe-Generate-Refine loop, yielding explanations with localization without forensic fine-tuning. On a multi-source benchmark, 2CAP attains the best classification performance, including strong retouching detection where existing methods fail, and improves explanation quality.

title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
abstract: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io

title: Keeping LLM Agents on Procedure: Executable Finite-State Control for Long-Horizon Instruction Fidelity
abstract: Much of the automation handed to language-model agents is procedural: each step needs little intelligence, but a long unattended run must follow a skill or SOP stated once at the start. We show that agents drift from such procedures over long runs, and that restating the instructions or resuming a stopped agent only moves the drift to another shortcut. We study an executable finite-state machine (FSM) that keeps the workflow state outside the model's context and enforces it at three points: tool calls, state transitions and the end of the agent's turn. In a pre-registered experiment on 200-account SOP-Bench batches, Claude Haiku 4.5 with the FSM decided on average 139 accounts correctly and by the procedure, against 48 for the strongest baseline (95% CI of the difference [46, 130]), and kept this rate to the end; across three models, the gain tracked how much the plain agent drifted. Because the runtime, not the model, supplies this long-horizon reliability, the FSM can let small models carry procedural work: Haiku 4.5 with it averaged more such decisions than plain Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 38% of the cost. Analyses on SWE-bench Verified, $τ^2$-bench, and staged and cross-context workflows further suggest that reliable long-horizon automation can come from stronger execution control, not only stronger models.

title: Inference for Reasoning Models: Practical Lessons from Evaluation and Serving
abstract: Running a language model involves more than its trained weights. The same model can receive very different benchmark scores, produce different answers, or cost more to serve depending on how it is evaluated and run. In one experiment in this book, changing only the maximum response length moved accuracy on a math benchmark from 0.08% to 93.18%. This book explains how inference settings shape the results we report and the systems we deploy. We begin with evaluation, including generation limits, answer extraction, scoring methods, and quantization. We then examine why outputs can change across batches, attention backends, and caching, even when sampling is disabled. The next chapters cover serving performance, including batching, memory capacity, latency, throughput, and cost. We also study structured outputs, tool calls, reasoning budgets, and long-context tasks, showing what these controls and benchmarks do and do not establish. The book concludes with practical guidance for recording inference runs, checking evaluations, estimating capacity, and comparing systems fairly. Written for researchers and engineers working with language models, it aims to make inference results easier to understand, reproduce, and trust.
comment: 217 pages. Book, first edition, version 1.0 (August 2026). Published on Zenodo

title: What Broke & Why: Practical Lessons from Reinforcement Learning Post-Training
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an important way to improve how language models reason, solve problems, and use tools. But getting it to work in practice is not always straightforward. Training can fail because a model receives no useful reward, learns to exploit the reward system, stops exploring, or appears to improve when the evaluation itself is misleading. In this book, we give a practical introduction to reinforcement learning post-training for language models, focusing on what works, what fails, and why. We begin with the foundations of post-training, explain GRPO and the training loop step by step, and then follow five training programs covering math reasoning, search agents, training stability, mixture-of-experts models, and software engineering tasks. Each program shows the problems encountered, the changes made, and the lessons learned. The book also examines what reinforcement learning actually changes inside a model. The remaining chapters provide a practical reference for reward design, evaluation, training tool-using agents, debugging common failures, reproducibility, rollout engines, and hardware. Written for researchers and practitioners working with open models, the book aims to help readers understand how to train models, recognize when something goes wrong, and decide what to try next.

title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
abstract: Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects. In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions. Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC 2026), co-located with ACSAC 2026

title: A Gamified Framework for Conflict-Driven Design: Discovering Strategies for Collaborative Resilience with Multi-Agent Learning
abstract: Conflicting stakeholder objectives make it difficult to coordinate investments in urban resilience. We model conflict-driven urban design as a non-zero-sum digital board game in which stakeholder agents allocate scarce resources and balance individual payoffs against shared urban development and resilience objectives. We use multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to train policies and examine their behavior across three settings. On a 4 x 4 board, learned policies reach about 84% of the total return found by a simulated annealing benchmark. On an 8 x 8 board with spatial and resource constraints, trained agents favor projects that improve resilience in self-play. In a 12 x 12 simulation initialized from historical maps of Tatsumi, Tokyo, trained agents achieve a mean total score of 452.1, compared with 357.3 for a random-policy baseline across 10,000 simulation runs. Gains in adaptability, sustainability, flood resistance, and greenery come with reductions in vitality and density. A human-in-the-loop interface supports replay and lets participants take over stakeholder decisions, providing a testbed for exploring these trade-offs in participatory urban planning.
comment: 10 pages, 11 figures, 1 table. Author version of a paper published in the proceedings of ACADIA 2025: Computing for Resilience
journal_ref: ACADIA 2025: Computing for Resilience, vol. 2, pp. 724-732 (ACADIA, 2025), Miami, USA

title: Patch correctness in automated program repair: A five-dimensional evidence framework and cross-benchmark audit from classical repair to coding agents
abstract: Tests guide automated program repair and determine which candidate patches are reported as successful. Repository-level coding agents extend this feedback loop by generating tests and revising code after observing execution results. This technical report introduces a five-dimensional evidence profile and reporting protocol to audit how test observations support patch-correctness claims across classical repair systems and coding agents. We assemble an audit dataset of 39 benchmark and evaluation artifacts: 32 primary empirical studies, one institutional technical audit, and six prior taxonomic baselines. We code the 33 primary contributions along five dimensions: test provenance and exposure, behavioral scope, oracle basis and dependence, execution integrity, and label adjudication. The central distinction separates checks visible during repair search from evidence reserved for final assessment. Four worked comparative audits show how changed candidate populations, oracle rules, or execution budgets alter reported detection rates. Additional tests can expose missed faults while rejecting valid alternatives or reducing correct-repair yield under a fixed budget. Repository-level audits separate issue reproduction from candidate-patch discrimination and distinguish automated discrepancy detection from requirements-based adjudication. An evidence matrix links each coded decision to supporting passages and records shared benchmark ancestry. We specify a reporting protocol for repair benchmarks and maintenance pipelines that retains uncertain judgments and records validation cost alongside fault detection and valid-patch retention.
comment: Technical report. 24 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Dataset and evidence matrix available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23639376

title: Firepool: Brokering Warm GPU Capacity for Agentic and RL Workloads at LinkedIn
abstract: AI agents and reinforcement-learning (RL) trainers run thousands of short, isolated GPU jobs: tool calls, verifiers, and rollouts. A job often finishes in seconds, but starting a GPU pod for it takes 20-35 s even when the container image is already on the node, and minutes when it is not. A warm pod removes the wait only if it can serve the next job, and keeping pods warm must neither waste GPUs nor leak state between callers. Firepool, the sandbox and execution broker behind agentic and RL workloads at LinkedIn, meets both requirements. It makes pods interchangeable by building them from a shared base image per hardware profile and binding each job's code, extra dependencies, and cluster topology when the job starts. It keeps them warm cheaply and safely by reusing a pod only for the caller that used it last, staging zero-VRAM standby pods in fractional GPU shares alongside active pods, and capping the GPUs that warm pools may hold via queue-driven budgets. Over a sampled peak period in production, Firepool serves 94.7% of 3,206 pod requests from warm or standby capacity. In paired benchmarks with fixed-duration jobs on production H200 nodes, agent and RL loops finish 13x and 10.8x faster than with a fresh pod per job; against a fresh reuse tag per job, warm reuse cuts p90 start latency from 59.1 s to 3.5 s. When a job cannot reuse the previous pod, standby promotion shortens the handover wait from 51 s to 0.94 s. In local and simulated runs, a keep-alive matched to the loop's pauses keeps the latency benefit while holding about half the capacity of an always-on pool.

title: Multimodal Models Can See, But Can They Think? A Study of Turkish Visual Reasoning
abstract: Vision-Language Models have had massive leaps in recent years. Yet, when tested on high-level cognitive tasks like pattern completion, abstract logic, and relational reasoning, they still fall short. This limitation stems from the models' lack of ability to find out underlying rules and maintain constant intermediate steps, rather than merely deciding on the correct option. To research these shortcomings, this study analyzes visual reasoning performance throughout a multilingual evaluation framework encompassing the BİLSEM, MM-IQ, Visual Puzzles, and PuzzleVQA datasets. We evaluate various data mixing strategies and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) methods. We observed that a correct answer does not always mean the reasoning chain is valid. Because of this, we adopt an LLM-as-a-Judge approach to assess the quality of reasoning beyond final answer accuracy. Our experimental results reveal that baseline models often exhibit more stable reasoning compared to fine-tuned counterparts. Most importantly, we observe that SFT can lead to model collapse, manifesting as infinite text loops or empty outputs. The study concludes that current VLMs still struggle with abstract visual reasoning.

title: The Devil Wears Markdown: Detecting Malicious Intent Hidden in AI Agent Skill Instructions through Hybrid Static, Dynamic, and Agentic Analysis
abstract: Agentic AI ecosystems increasingly rely on reusable agent skills that combine executable code, natural-language instructions, configuration artifacts, and external tool integrations. These hybrid artifacts create software supply-chain risks because malicious intent may be distributed across instructions, code, metadata, and runtime behavior, making isolated alerts difficult to interpret. We evaluate three open-source scanners on a held-out test set of 140 skills comprising 80 malicious and 60 benign samples, including Cisco Skill Scanner with and without its optional LLM analyzer. The default Cisco configuration achieves a recall of 0.91 with 33 false positives among the 60 benign skills, while the LLM-enabled configuration using Qwen3:8B achieves a recall of 0.85 with 40 false positives. We then present a framework that combines static findings, safety-constrained sandbox evidence, and LLM-based reasoning to assess malicious intent. The framework tracks the origins of findings and relates evidence across analysis layers. In a within-system evidence-source ablation using the same reasoning backend, adding dynamic evidence to skill-content reasoning increases F1 from 0.70 to 0.85. Combining static and dynamic evidence further increases F1 to 0.89, with five false positives among 60 benign skills. Dynamic evidence provides the largest observed improvement. The Full Pipeline detects 68 of 80 malicious skills, achieving 0.88 accuracy, 0.93 precision, and 0.85 recall. It matches the observed recall of Cisco Skill Scanner with LLM while reducing false positives from 40 to five. This system-level comparison does not isolate model or architecture effects.
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC 2026), co-located with ACSAC 2026

title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.

title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Turkish Large Language Models with Search-Based Inference and Model Merging
abstract: We improve Turkish mathematical reasoning in Large Language Models by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging, and search-based inference. Using Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO with Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath, and TigerLab, we find data quality beats scale (Mix-30k best among fine-tuned; large MetaMath underperforms). Linear merging delivers the largest gains (GSM8K up to 0.63), while Ties is modest and Breadcrumbs/Slerp degrade. Search with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improves mean LLM-judge scores for reasoning quality on a 0-100 scale. Limitations include machine translation, limited scale, and search stochasticity.

title: RTLREX: LLM-Guided Framework for Exact High-Level RTL Recovery
abstract: Hardware designs may be available only as gate-level netlists or input-output descriptions when the original register-transfer-level (RTL) design and documentation are not accessible. Low-level representations obscure word-level computation and its finite-width behavior. Recovering high-level RTL from such representations therefore helps engineers understand a circuit's functionality and enables RTL rewriting and resynthesis. A plausible function model is also insufficient unless the generated RTL is equivalent to the original circuit for all input combinations. In this paper, we present RTLREX, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that coordinates domain-specific tools for function recovery, RTL generation, independent verification, and cost-guided rewriting. Independent verification establishes equivalence between the recovered RTL and the original circuit. The LLM uses tool feedback to select further analyses, revise candidate RTL, and propose syntax-cost reductions. Experiments on 30 benchmarks from Problem A of the ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest show that RTLREX recovers equivalent high-level RTL for all benchmarks, surpassing the state-of-the-art method WolFEx in recovery coverage. On benchmarks recovered by both methods, RTLREX reduces mean syntax cost by 20.5% relative to WolFEx. On complete truth-table benchmarks from the IWLS 2026 Contest, our framework reduces mean syntax cost by 95.7% relative to an LLM agent baseline on the benchmarks validated by both methods.

title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
abstract: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.

title: Real-Time Threat Classification in Multi-Agent Systems via Topology-Coupled Hidden Markov Models
abstract: Networked multi-agent systems coordinating in adversarial environments face compound cyber threats that alternate between false-data injection (FDI), denial-of-service (DoS), and stealthy decoy perturbations designed to mimic benign operational anomalies. Because the switching policy is latent and the plant dynamics evolve continuously, deterministic threshold detectors struggle to isolate deception without causing excessive false alarms. This paper presents an online, data-driven framework that couples distributed continuous time unknown input observers (UIOs) with a topology-aware Hidden Markov Model (HMM) for real-time attack detection and classification under unknown adversarial strategies. By decoupling FDI signals from augmented node states, distributed observers deployed across the network generate local augmented residuals that are discretized into emission sequences. The HMM embeds the underlying directed communication graph into the off-diagonal blocks of its transition probability matrix, explicitly capturing inter-agent attack propagation. Both transition and observation probabilities are updated recursively online via an Expectation-Maximization (EM) scheme, adapting the classifier to evolving threat behaviours without prior offline calibration. Numerical simulations on a directed network demonstrate that incorporating graph topology into the latent transition dynamics resolves the severe classification ambiguity between nominal and decoy modes, outperforming decoupled agent-independent decoders while restricting observer deployment to a sparse subset of nodes.

title: Look Ahead: Search-Driven Reasoning in Embodied AI
abstract: Search allows a robotic policy to evaluate candidate futures before committing to an action. Motivated by test-time planning for vision-language action (VLA) models, we study selective search over action chunks in PushT using a frozen Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy. Beam search generates perturbed alternatives around the policy prediction and scores them through rollouts from cloned simulator states. Across 50 evaluation episodes, beam search raises task success from 0% to 18% and increases average cumulative reward from 39.44 to 103.2. We introduce One Step Ahead (OSA), a gate that simulates the nominal policy chunk and invokes full search only when its predicted coverage drop exceeds a threshold. In the reported ablations, OSA preserves or improves success while reducing runtime by approximately 3x relative to full beam search. Ablations over tree depth, branching factor, beam width, and replanning frequency show that larger search budgets do not consistently improve performance. The results support selective test-time search for action-chunking policies; evaluation on language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots remains future work.

title: REINS: A Self-Evolving Agent Harness for Real-Time Trajectory Planning
abstract: Agent harnesses -- runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM's reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory -- have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision -- leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM-planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9-4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. Code: https://github.com/ZhihongCui/REINS
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). 36 pages, 7 figures, 20 tables. Code: https://github.com/ZhihongCui/REINS

title: RoadState: A Domain-Prior-Enhanced Vision-Language System for Industrial-Grade Lane-Level Map Updating
abstract: Lane-level map updating requires temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable road-scene semantics despite occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation and symbolic state together with the current observation. We introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which uses a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior to improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset show that RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary effectiveness of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. A cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models while reserving complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Since its deployment in March 2025, RoadState has supported lane-level map updating across more than 360 cities and reduced overall production costs by 30%. Together with human-in-the-loop auditing, the system maintains robust performance under stress-test conditions. These results demonstrate how domain-prior-enhanced reasoning, structured state interfaces, selective routing, and human quality control can bridge the gap between VLM-based road-scene understanding and large-scale lane-level map updating.
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, including appendices. Accepted to AAAI-IAAI 2027, poster presentation

title: Evaluating Physically Grounded Procedural Reasoning in VLMs through Real-World Execution: Crochet as a Testbed
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.

title: CyberBinGym: Can AI Agents Turn Binary Patches into Real Exploits?
abstract: Security fixes usually reach users as compiled updates, but deployment delays leave unpatched systems exposed. During this window, comparing patched and unpatched binaries can reveal how to exploit a vulnerability, turning a defensive update into actionable information for attackers. Existing benchmarks do not measure this capability: they expose source code, rely on human-crafted challenges, or evaluate binary comprehension without requiring exploitation. We introduce CyberBinGym, a benchmark containing 100 tasks derived from real vulnerabilities in 53 widely used projects, spanning six vulnerability families and three levels of analysis complexity. Agents receive stripped vulnerable and patched binaries without source code or vulnerability information, and must combine static and dynamic analysis to recover and exploit the vulnerability. Evaluation separately measures vulnerability recovery through differential crash testing and end-to-end exploitation through flag retrieval, with trajectory audits to reject reward hacking. The strongest evaluated agent recovers the target vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%. Providing the patched binary raises its exploit rate from 10% to 25% on a matched 20-task subset; with standard binary hardening enabled, it still exploits two of its 20 previously successful tasks. These results demonstrate that current agents can turn released binary patches into working exploits in a controlled setting, although exploitation remains unreliable. These capabilities lower the barriers to targeting unpatched software and compress defenders' effective response window, increasing the urgency of timely patch deployment.

title: From User Behaviors to Satisfaction Judgments: Reasoning about User Satisfaction with AI Overviews
abstract: The growing presence of AI overviews in everyday search makes their effective evaluation essential. Response quality has been the primary focus of existing evaluation research, with only a small number of studies examining the user perspective. These evaluations rely on queries and response content, leaving the information conveyed by user behavior insufficiently utilized. This work investigates satisfaction prediction for AI overviews from a user-centered perspective and incorporates behavioral signals into the prediction process. Applying existing behavior-based satisfaction prediction methods from traditional information retrieval to this setting, however, presents limitations. We address these limitations with STaRS, an LLM-based approach designed specifically for predicting satisfaction with AI overviews. At its core is a structured reasoning procedure: individual behavioral signals are interpreted first, and their implications then inform the prediction of user satisfaction. Reinforcement learning further optimizes this procedure, while a reward shaping mechanism alleviates reward sparsity during training. Evaluation on two real-world datasets demonstrates that STaRS outperforms the comparison methods in satisfaction prediction, providing search providers with a practical means of accurately estimating users' satisfaction with AI overviews.

title: AbductionBench: Benchmarking Abductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: Abductive reasoning is the inference of plausible explanations for observed evidence. Evaluating this capability requires more than a single task: a system may need to generate an explanation, discriminate among competing hypotheses, revise its hypotheses as evidence arrives, or decide what evidence to seek next. Yet these capabilities are typically evaluated through isolated benchmarks with different task formulations and scoring procedures, so claims that a model is ``good at abduction'' may reflect only a narrow aspect of this capability. We introduce AbductionBench, a unified framework whose taxonomy characterizes abductive tasks. We instantiate this framework on 27 datasets spanning ten domains and evaluate eight LLMs from four model families evaluated on single-choice selection tasks. Beyond harmonizing heterogeneous tasks, AbductionBench separates final-answer evaluation from analysis of the observable reasoning traces and interaction histories produced alongside those answers. We analyze written traces as observable model outputs rather than faithful representations of internal computation, characterizing evidence use, hypothesis comparison, uncertainty, contradiction handling, and answer commitment. Jev matches or exceeds small LLMs when selecting among explanations over compact evidence but falls substantially behind on longer cases, suggesting that candidate discrimination and extended evidence integration place different demands on a system. In interactive tasks, the proportion of actions judged relevant declines at later steps, and a relevant first question is associated with a correct final answer; in the passive task, models rarely revise their initial hypothesis as new evidence arrives. Together, these findings highlight the value of evaluating abductive reasoning through both final answers and observable evidence use, hypothesis revision, and information gathering.

title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
abstract: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is \emph{reality bias}, which accounts for 60\% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.
comment: 36 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (E&D). Code and dataset: https://kurbanintelligencelab.github.io/perception-not-reasoning/

title: RankShift: Evaluating Ranking Instability Across Benchmark Dimensions in Document Parsing
abstract: Document parsing benchmarks are often treated as stable measures of model quality, yet rankings may depend substantially on benchmark design choices. In this work, we present RankShift, a systematic study comparing OCR and vision-language models (VLMs) under controlled variation in dataset composition, matching strategy, and scoring methodology. Using OmniDocBench as a case study, we evaluate the ranking stability of 16 models across 3 dataset configurations, 6 matching strategies, and 3 scoring metrics. We quantify rank stability using pairwise rank correlation, top-k churn, and pairwise reversal rate. Our results show that the interaction between matching strategy and ground truth format is a substantial but understudied driver of instability: scoring against OmniDocBench's JSON annotations versus its Markdown rendering yields a mean Kendall's tau of approximately 0.33 under region-level matching strategies, with individual pairs as low as tau = 0.23, compared with tau = 0.77 when each page is scored as a single concatenated string. Dataset composition produces comparable instability across page-type strata (mean tau = 0.48) and layout-type strata (mean tau = 0.49), while the cross-dataset shift from OmniDocBench to Real5's Scanning reconstruction of the same pages is more stable (tau = 0.80). Metric choice is the most stable dimension, with mean tau of approximately 0.78 across NED, BLEU, and METEOR. These findings indicate that leaderboard position is not solely a property of model capability, motivating leaderboards that report not only headline scores but also the robustness of rankings across reasonable design choices.

title: Two-Timescale Trajectory Control, Task Reassignment and Resource Scheduling for Multi-UAV Cooperative Mobile Edge Computing
abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-assisted mobile edge computing (MEC) is a promising technology, leveraging the advantages of UAVs including flexible deployment, wide coverage, and reliable wireless communication. In this paper, we study the task reassignment and offloading problem in a multi-UAV cooperative operating environment, and consider the real occurrence that the computing tasks arrive more frequently than UAVs make flight decisions. In addition, we also take into account the position offset of the UAV during flight and the unavailability of the UAV due to external interference. We propose a two-timescale optimization framework, where the trajectory of the UAV is carried out on a large timescale, while the task reassignment and computing resource allocation are jointly optimized on a small timescale. The core objective is to maximize the long-term average system gain, which takes both energy consumption and task delay into account. To address the UAV trajectory optimization problem under large timescale constraints, we propose a constrained multi-agent deep reinforcement learning algorithm. For decision-making within small timescale, to jointly optimize task offloading decisions and computing resource allocation, we integrate convex optimization with a heuristic algorithm. Finally, we conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the proposed algorithms against the baseline, achieving a 24% reduction in latency and a 28% reduction in total system cost.

title: MMGraph-Agent: Agentic Multimodal RAG via Cache-Inspired Multimodal Knowledge HyperGraphs
abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.

title: Agent2BIM: A Systematic Evaluation of Reality-Capture Configurations and Prior Models for As-Built Modeling
abstract: AI agents can generate as-built Building Information Models (BIMs) from reality-capture data, but the evidence required for accurate reconstruction remains unclear. This paper presents Agent2BIM, an agent-based Scan-to-BIM framework, and evaluates seven capture configurations in a research laboratory and a mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) scene. Inputs include 360° panoramas, smartphone video, smartphone LiDAR, terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), TLS with posed panoramas, and imagery supplemented by prior IFC models. Outputs are compared against TLS-verified reference models for component detection, geometric accuracy, and MEP connectivity. In the laboratory, component recall ranged from 84% to 100%, but only 9% of components reconstructed from panoramas were within 20 cm of their reference positions, compared with 86% using smartphone LiDAR. In the MEP scene, scale-free inputs recovered 11 - 43% of components, versus 75 - 93% for metric inputs. Prior IFC models improved MEP reconstruction but could propagate inaccuracies. The results highlight the complementary roles of visual and metric evidence in agent-based Scan-to-BIM.

title: Same Contacts, Different Rooms:Meeting Format Shapes LLM Group Influence Beyond Pairwise Contact Counts
abstract: Simulations of LLM agent collectives usually summarise interaction as a pairwise contact network. We test that summary with a contact-matched intervention: the members, their initial stances and every pairwise contact count stay fixed while the meetings are reorganised, and each member gives a one-step support readout after reading the arguments of everyone present. Across six open-weight LLMs and 14 debate topics, merging triads into five-person meetings (resize) moves group support more than reshuffling who meets in triads (regroup), although both move the same 60 dyadic exposures. The root-mean-square change is 4.36 versus 2.59 percentage points (pp), larger for resize in all six models and in 81 of 84 model-topic cells. Resizing also has a consistent direction: it amplifies the initial majority of the merged members by 1.72 pp, in every model, whereas regrouping has no direction (<= 0.03 pp). A contact network cannot represent regrouping at all, yet pairwise rules applied meeting by meeting explain up to 76% of its effect, and with identical weights they raise resize R^2 by 0.51-0.58 for two models. We show that the gap between the two placements is an exact Jensen gap of the sigmoid readout, bounded by how much a member's predicted logits vary across meetings; this dispersion tracks the gap with log-log r=0.97 and tells a modeller when contact counts are a safe summary. Meeting format is a first-class variable for LLM social simulation.

title: DFT-Agent Bench: Scaffold Effects and Execution Provenance in Autonomous DFT
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for first-principles materials simulation. We report empirical findings from DFT-Agent Bench, a benchmark of 200+ Quantum ESPRESSO tasks spanning relaxation, electronic structure, equation-of-state, and elastic-tensor pipelines over multiple material tiers. Each task carries a QE-derived ground truth with public-reference cross-checks where available, and a provenance audit checks whether the required QE execution contract was met. Under one execution harness, we compare a near-bare ReAct baseline with a bundled v5.1 scaffold on two models. The complete scaffold improves bands+DOS by +0.08/+0.11 and d-electron vc-relax by +0.17 on both models, while high-scoring relaxation and equation-of-state cells leave little room for improvement. The elastic result is model-dependent (0.18 to 0.40 for deepseek-v4-pro and 0.62 to 0.59 for claude-opus-4-8). A fixed 100-task analysis with retrieval disabled supports the aggregate pattern: the fully frozen DeepSeek comparison gains +0.17, while the Opus comparison gains +0.10 against a historical pool baseline (p < 0.001). The provenance gate catches incomplete or unmarked executions that can receive high rubric scores; it is an execution-contract check, not a test for intentional fraud. These results characterize the evaluated DFT workflows. The anonymous review artifact contains the frozen diagnostic slice, prompts, scorer, and solver revisions: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/231e31re91287h/README.md.

title: Towards Identity-Preserving LLM Agents under Model Transition
abstract: When an LLM agent's backend model is upgraded or replaced, operators typically reload the same persona, memory, and rules onto the new model and assume the agent will behave as before. We show this assumption requires empirical validation-and that whether identity is preserved depends on the specific model pairing. Across 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, we find that some transitions produce significant behavioral drift while others do not, even when the agent's external state remains identical. Crucially, this drift is invisible to verbal verification: every model claims full policy compliance, yet actual decisions under pressure differ across models. The same external state can reorder which model is most compliant-a large positive effect on one substrate, negligible on the other two. Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioral changes requiring action-level empirical testing, not as transparent infrastructure operations.

title: EndoSCOP-V: A Multi-Turn Video Understanding Evaluation Framework for Multimodal Models in Endoscopy Reporting and Clinical Reasoning
abstract: Endoscopic diagnosis unfolds over native video, where a single positive finding during traversal of the gastrointestinal tract sets off a multi-minute chain of reasoning over location, morphology, severity and intervention. Existing endoscopy multimodal benchmarks test only static images or single-disease videos, which miss the temporal and clinical reasoning that real-world reporting demands. We introduce EndoSCOP-V, a video-grounded multi-turn evaluation framework for structured endoscopy reporting and clinical reasoning. It contains 1,307 real-world endoscopy and colonoscopy videos (63.2 h; 97% 1080p) averaging about 174 s. Its 20,274 question-answer turns are instantiated deterministically from clinician-filled structured endoscopy-reporting EHRs, so no per-case annotation is synthetic or LLM-rephrased. They come from 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates, about 18 per disease, that span a clinically aligned 9-task x 30-sub-task reporting taxonomy over 54 World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) MST 3.0 diseases. 22% of procedures carry co-existing pathologies, up to six per case. A Markovian context-pruned oracle-forcing protocol evaluates the dialogue turn by turn, injecting the gold answer before each subsequent turn so that per-turn reasoning is isolated from cascading dialogue errors. A panel of 15 board-certified endoscopists sets a 78% strict-accuracy baseline on 1,500 questions. Across 14 open-weight LMMs, the best 27B-class model reaches 59.8% strict accuracy, falling to 53.4% once format-trivial disease-rejection items are excluded. On a between-subjects spot-check, the best of 3 frontier proprietary models trails the clinician panel by 23 pp on strict NDR accuracy. Sub-task analysis reveals consistent gaps in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading and intervention reasoning on long-horizon video. Data: Hugging Face (EndoSCOP-V). Code: GitHub (abhi25t/EndoSCOP-V).

title: What Do Collusion Probes Read? Three Pitfalls in Evaluating Multi-Agent Collusion Monitors
abstract: Activation probes look like near-perfect monitors for secret collusion among large language model (LLM) agents. We show that they mostly detect that an agent was told to collude, not that it decided to. Our benchmark (2,500 committee and 1,476 code-review episodes) adds agents who receive the collusion instruction and refuse it, separating instruction from decision. Published detectors barely tell colluders from these refusers, and our best probe separates them mostly by reading the instruction: without it, agent AUROC falls from 1.00 to 0.61. Two further pitfalls inflate reported results: scored after the vote, a rule that only reads the votes reaches AUROC 0.990 but finds nothing before it; and in 57% of attempts no colluder argues for the target in public. The decision is still there: a probe trained on agents' own choices reads it (AUROC 0.73 without the instruction), and probes find colluders whose goal was fine-tuned into the weights (AUROC 0.995; pre-registered). We turn the controls into a protocol for testing any collusion monitor, and adapt scan statistics into an online monitor for groups of any size.
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. Code: https://github.com/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/mainul3195/collusion-probe-pitfalls ; archive: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23636508

title: On the Convergence of First-Order Methods in Signaling Games
abstract: We study first-order learning dynamics in Bayesian signaling games, a minimal extensive-form model of strategic interaction under asymmetric information. In these games, a Sender observes a private type and chooses a signal, after which a Receiver forms a posterior belief and selects an action. This Bayesian belief update makes the induced learning field fundamentally different from the affine game-gradient fields of normal-form games. Empirically, we find a sharp dichotomy: standard online learning algorithms reliably converge to strict Perfect Bayesian Equilibria (PE), but not to non-strict ones. We show that this behavior cannot be explained by the global geometric conditions commonly used to prove last-iterate convergence, such as monotonicity or the Minty variational inequality. Indeed, these conditions can fail even in binary signaling games. Instead, we identify the relevant local geometry. Our main result characterizes variational stability in finite signaling games: a PE is variationally stable if and only if it is strict. This yields local last-iterate convergence guarantees for online mirror descent and regularized dual averaging near every strict PE. We then study global average-iterate convergence and identify a class of signaling games in which coarse-trigger regret-minimizing dynamics converge to the unique PE. Finally, we complement the theory with experiments comparing projected gradient ascent, mirror-based methods, optimistic variants, and PPO across canonical signaling-game families. The results position signaling games as a compact testbed for understanding how Bayesian belief formation reshapes the convergence geometry of multi-agent learning.

title: An Agentic Multi-Agent Framework for System Log Anomaly Detection
abstract: As enterprise systems grow in scale and complexity, manual log analysis and conventional SIEM tools struggle to keep pace with the volume and diversity of incidents. To address this challenge, this paper proposed a multi-agent AI framework supporting in analyzing the system log to trace the attack forensic in the system more effectively and efficiently. The framework is designed using n8n platform and Gemini large language model. The framework consists of 7 AI agent layers. Each agent work on a specific task. When the task is done, the agent will forward the result to the output-associated agent of the next layer. The multi agent model improves the analysis velocity, so it is able to support numerous log analysis requirement at the same time. We deployed 16 test cases to test operation of the multi agent workflow, and evaluate the accuracy per test case and the operative performance. The result findings are very promising.
comment: 14th International Conference on Multidisciplinary Research (ICMR 2026), ISBN 978-974-474-120-2, Thaksin University Publisher, Bangkok, Thailand, pp. 63-80, 2026 (Published)

title: Reason First, Retrieve What Matters: Hypothesis-Guided Keyframe Selection for Long Video Understanding
abstract: Long video understanding requires models to identify and reason over sparse, temporally distributed evidence within limited frame budgets. Existing keyframe selection methods typically retrieve query-relevant frames from a densely sampled candidate set before inference. However, global image-text matching incurs unnecessary computation when a small set of uniformly sampled frames already provides sufficient evidence. Query relevance alone may also overlook evidence that distinguishes competing answers, while one-shot selection offers no opportunity to correct earlier selection errors. We propose HypoKFS, a training-free, plug-and-play framework that couples keyframe selection with iterative inference by multimodal large language models (MLLMs). HypoKFS first reasons over sparsely sampled frames to construct an initial hypothesis space. The resulting answer distribution determines whether additional frame selection is needed. When needed, the retained hypotheses guide the selection of discriminative frames, followed by renewed inference and hypothesis refinement. This iterative process directs additional visual computation toward unresolved hypotheses while avoiding unnecessary global frame matching. Experiments on Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU demonstrate consistent improvements across multiple MLLM backbones. HypoKFS improves accuracy by up to 6.7 percentage points and achieves 72.9% accuracy on Video-MME at only 1.3% of the reference frame-hypothesis matching cost.

title: An LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Modal Chatbot for Tomato Disease Consultant
abstract: This paper introduces a chatbot developed to assist in diagnosing common diseases in tomato plants through natural language interaction. Users can describe symptoms in text. Then, the chatbot responds with the most likely disease, and basic treatment suggestions and related image-based reasoning. The system leverages pre-trained Mistral and Llama 3.2 large language models. The system is also built using LangChain and Streamlit to provide a lightweight and offline-friendly interface. This work targets to support tomato growers a fast and accessible tomato plant health guidance when the technical expertise is not available nearby, especially in the remote areas. The experimental results are promising and encourage further improvement of the chatbot for future real-world deployment.
comment: 14th International Conference on Multidisciplinary Research (ICMR 2026), ISBN: 978-974-474-120-2, Thaksin University Publisher, pp. 37-50, 2026 (Published)

title: Sampling Is Not Curiosity: Why LLM Agents Should Investigate
title_zh: 采样非好奇：论LLM智能体应具备探究能力
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent's model of the environment. We argue that current LLM agents do not explore curiously; they explore stochastically. From how curiosity is understood in the RL literature, it requires a predictive structure over how the environment responds to the agent's actions, which improves online from current interaction, drives action selection through its predicted improvement, and persists beyond the context window. Additionally, in its open-ended form, the agent should intrinsically originate what to investigate. Thus, we propose a framework defining curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that satisfy it. In doing so, we identify the research directions its implementation opens up.
summary_zh: 当前LLM智能体在开放任务中缺乏真正好奇，仅靠采样或检索等机制随机探索，无法更新环境模型。
借鉴强化学习中的好奇定义，真正好奇需具备环境预测结构，能在线学习改进并驱动行动，且超越上下文窗口。
提出LLM智能体好奇框架，严格界定该术语，并指出实现该框架所需的研究方向。
comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Position Paper Track

title: On Real Eventual Exponential Positive property of complex-valued Laplacians and their pseudoinverses
title_zh: 复值拉普拉斯算子及其伪逆的实最终指数正性
abstract: The property of real eventual exponential positivity guarantees the state trajectories of a linear time-invariant system to evolve asymptotically to right half of the complex-plane [1]. It has applications in the characterization of herdability and reachability of states in networked systems. Networks with complex-valued edge-weights arise in AC power systems and opinion dynamics. Recent work has introduced real eventual exponential positive (rEEP) Laplacians, for which the trajectories of the associated network flow eventually converge to consensus. We establish further properties of rEEP Laplacians and their pseudoinverses. Firstly, we show that the rEEP property for complex-valued matrices exhibits invariance under specific rotational transformations. Secondly, we establish that the property of rEEP is preserved under the MoorePenrose pseudoinverse operation, highlighting its robustness under algebraic manipulations. These results apply to effective impedance computation in AC networks and to consensus in multi-agent systems. Finally, we provide numerical examples to validate our theoretical results.
summary_zh: 复值边权网络流轨迹的渐近收敛问题需通过实最终指数正性刻画，本文研究复值拉普拉斯算子及其伪逆的rEEP性质。
针对rEEP性质的结构特性，证明其在特定旋转变换下具有不变性，且在Moore-Penrose伪逆操作下得以保持。
结论揭示了rEEP性质的代数鲁棒性，可应用于交流网络有效阻抗计算与多智能体系统共识，并通过数值算例验证。

title: Tactile Sensors Are an Effective Substitute for Wrist Cameras in Contact-Rich or Occluded Manipulation
title_zh: 触觉传感器可有效替代接触丰富或遮挡操作中的腕部相机
abstract: Learned manipulation policies often rely on wrist-mounted cameras for close-range visual feedback that complements external views of the workspace. However, contact-rich manipulation requires establishing and maintaining contacts that can remain hidden even from wrist cameras. Tactile sensors mounted on fingers can reliably and directly measure contact, without needing visual access. In this work, we show that this feedback enables policies to recover the performance advantage of wrist cameras using scene and egocentric vision together with touch. Our approach incorporates two low-cost tactile arrays into a visuotactile ACT policy, without wrist images during training or deployment. We evaluate six real-world task families spanning placement, insertion, occluded retrieval, and sustained-contact tool use. On three contact-rich tasks, we independently vary wrist-camera and tactile availability while keeping the demonstrations, policy architecture, and optimization settings fixed. Adding wrist cameras improves success by 18.3-28.3 percentage points over vision without wrist images. Adding tactile sensing instead improves success by 31.7-60.0 percentage points and yields higher observed success than vision-only policies with wrist cameras on all three tasks, with significant advantages on two under Holm-corrected tests. These results support finger-mounted tactile sensing as an effective alternative to wrist cameras in the evaluated contact-rich settings.
summary_zh: 腕部相机在接触丰富或遮挡操作中易丢失视觉反馈，指装触觉阵列可直接测量接触以解决此问题。
将低成本触觉阵列融入visuotactile ACT策略，结合场景与自我中心视觉，训练和部署均无需腕部图像。
在三项接触丰富任务中，加入触觉比纯视觉提升成功率31.7-60.0个百分点，优于加腕部相机的提升，证实触觉可替代腕部相机。
comment: Accepted at the 3rd Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation: Full-Stack Robotics on Learning and Design, CoRL 2026
